sets.title: Turn It Down: Is Your Music Too Loud?

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared in a magazine for young people:
partA.title: Turn It Down: Is Your Music Too Loud?
partA.text:
Earphones have become part of daily life for most teenagers. We wear them on the bus and even in bed. But medical experts are increasingly concerned that many young people are slowly damaging their hearing without knowing it.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), more than one billion young people around the world are at risk of hearing loss because they listen to loud sounds too often and for too long. The WHO says that listening at 85 decibels for eight hours, or at 100 decibels for just 15 minutes, can be harmful. Loud sound may first cause only a short ringing in the ears, but repeated exposure can make hearing loss permanent.

"The problem is that the damage happens quietly," explains Dr Helen Marsh, an audiologist who checks patients' hearing. "There is no pain, so at first you might only notice a ringing in your ears after a concert, or you keep asking friends to repeat themselves in a noisy restaurant."

So why do people turn the volume up? Some want to block out the noise of traffic or trains, while others say loud music helps them concentrate or feel more energetic. Sixteen-year-old Leo admits he often listens at full volume. "If I can still hear people talking around me, it isn't loud enough," he says.

Dr Marsh recommends a simple '60/60 rule': listen at no more than 60% of the maximum volume, for no more than 60 minutes at a time.

However, not all teenagers agree. "My grandparents can't hear well, and they never used earphones," says Leo. "I'll worry about it when I'm older."

sets.title: Fast Forward: Young Viewers Hit the Speed Button

partA.sourceIntro: This article appeared in a local newspaper:
partA.title: Fast Forward: Young Viewers Hit the Speed Button
partA.text:
When Form 5 student Chloe Tam sits down to watch a drama, she rarely watches it at normal speed. "I usually choose 1.5 times, sometimes double speed," she explains. "That way, I can finish a whole series in a weekend and still have time for homework."

Chloe is not alone. Most video apps now allow viewers to change the playback speed, and a survey of 600 local secondary students by the youth group Teen Screen Lab found that 58% often watch dramas or online videos faster than normal. Among these speed-watchers, the most common reasons were saving time (71%) and skipping 'boring' parts (45%). Students could give more than one reason.

Supporters say speed-watching is efficient and helps busy students keep up with popular shows, so they can join conversations with their friends. Some also use it when they revise with online lessons. "A recorded lesson that takes an hour only takes 40 minutes at 1.5 times," says one university student.

However, not everyone is a fan. A local film lecturer believes viewers miss a great deal. "Directors use silence, music and the expressions on actors' faces to tell a story. When you rush, you only follow the plot, not the emotions," he says. Some teachers also worry that students who speed through lessons may remember less, and that the habit is making young people less patient.

Chloe disagrees. "If a show is really good, I slow down and enjoy every scene. Speed is just a tool," she says.

So, is pressing the speed button a smart way to use our time, or are we losing something important?

sets.title: Strangers Next Door? Four Ways to Get to Know Your Neighbours

partA.sourceIntro: This list of tips appeared on a website for Hong Kong families:
partA.title: Strangers Next Door? Four Ways to Get to Know Your Neighbours
partA.text:
In a city where thousands of people can live in one building, many of us do not even know the names of the people next door. A recent survey by this website found that only one in four readers could name a neighbour on their floor. Yet good neighbours can help in an emergency, look after your flat when you are away, or simply make home feel friendlier. A smile and a 'good morning' in the lift is a good start, but here are four ideas that can bring the neighbours in a housing estate together.

1. Start a floor group chat
A group chat lets neighbours share news quickly, such as lift repairs or lost keys. Remember to set some rules so that it does not become too noisy, and help older residents who are not used to smartphones to join.

2. Set up a swap shelf
Put a small shelf in a shared area where people can leave books, toys or kitchen items they no longer need, and take something else in return. It saves money and reduces waste.

3. Organise a festival party
Mid-Autumn Festival and Lunar New Year are perfect times to invite neighbours to share snacks, make lanterns or decorate the building together.

4. Share your skills
Can you fix computers, cook a special dish or help children with homework? A weekly 'skill swap' lets neighbours teach each other something useful for free.
